newsitem.title: UK: Colombia austerity cuts little ice with investors.
newsitem.headline: Colombia austerity cuts little ice with investors.

text.p: Colombia's announcement of an economic emergency package to slash its fiscal deficit has so far cut little ice with foreign investors, who said on Tuesday they feared the process may deepen political unrest.

Colombian President Ernesto Samper on Monday decreed a 20-day economic emergency which allows the government to introduce measures without the approval of Congress, and signalled the need for urgent belt-tightening measures.

Colombia's unions, fearing the government will use its crisis powers to cut up to 19,000 state jobs, now plan to bring forward nationwide strikes prompted by sub-inflation pay rises, and investors fear more social strife ahead.
"I don't think the news is all that favourable," said Joe MacHatton, Latin American strategist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson (DKB).

"The reason is that the problems in Colombia are a little longer term and have to do with the fight against the drug cartels and money diverted outside the economy, and these will still be there in 1997."
Colombia has been fighting a dual battle against drug barons and left-wing guerrillas that has been absorbing an increasing proportion of its gross domestic product.
Coupled with this is an economic slowdown highlighted by October's industrial output figures that were down 7.85 percent year-on-year.
At about 2.5 percent of GDP, Colombia's government deficit is one of the highest in Latin America after Brazil's 3.5.

While all the details of the austerity package have yet to be announced, Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said on Monday that Colombia would drastically cut its foreign debt programme and impose a new tax on firms that contracted fresh foreign debt.

On Friday Ocampo announced separately that public sector workers would get a 13.5 percent wage rise, well below government inflation forecasts of 18 percent and analysts' expectations of 20 percent for 1997.
Unions already gearing up to strike are now doubly concerned at what else might be imposed under the emergency powers.
Investors are worried about Colombia's fiscal deficit and its impact on inflation, but they also say the government should be wary of provoking political unrest.
"Reduce it, but be selective about how you do it, and don't create social strains," said Suzanne Carrington, Latin American portfolio manager at Flemings Investment Management.

But Carrington said Colombia ought also to consider cutting the deficit via stepping up privatisation, especially of the state telecoms company, and should address spending by its state governments -- a problem Colombia also shares with Brazil.
Frederique Carrier, Colombia analyst at brokerage BBV LatInvest, and DKB's MacHatton agreed the rebel problem was also a major contributer to the fiscal problems.

"If they are going to reduce the overall level of government spending there will have to be cuts in its police and military operations, or in government help to people affected," MacHatton said. "Whichever end it is it will have an adverse effect."

After lagging last year, Colombia has been Latin America's best performing market over the first two weeks of 1997, the Bogota stock market rallying 17.6 percent compared with its nearest competitor Brazil, up just 9.06 percent.

Some foreign investors are starting to want to take profits and fund managers say they will weigh cutting their exposure if social unrest hots up. Others will not put new money in until the situation clarifies.
"Colombia is a market performer -- it is too early to be selling but I wouldn't be putting money into it right now," MacHatton said. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
